0.question: What is epidermolytic hyperkeratosis and how does it affect the palms and soles?

final_answer.long_answer: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is an autosomal-dominant form of congenital ichthyosis caused by mutations in the KRT1 or KRT10 genes that weaken suprabasal keratin filaments. Affected newborns blister easily; with time the damaged epidermis responds by producing marked hyperkeratosis. On the palms and soles, where keratin 1 is highly expressed, this manifests as thick, ridged, yellow-brown palmoplantar keratoderma that may crack and impair function.

llm.short_answer: A rare genetic skin disorder marked by abnormal cornification that causes thickening of the skin, including severe hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles when keratin 1 is affected.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_15], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1]. Detailed explanation: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is a rare autosomal dominant disorder of cornification caused by mutations in keratin genes, specifically keratin 1 and keratin 10. It is also known as bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma. The disorder is characterized by the clumping of keratin filaments, leading to skin fragility initially, followed by the development of hyperkeratosis. Notably, the form associated with keratin 1 mutations results in significant thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, whereas mutations in keratin 10 typically do not affect these areas.

Section: Introduction
Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI),[a] is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures, strong body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] The two main types are divided into one involving palms and soles and the other without.[6] EI is caused by a genetic mutation.[6] The condition involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[5][6] The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
EI is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures,  body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] Complications include infection and joint problems.[6] Affected newborns are particularly at risk of dehydration, sepsis, and electrolyte imbalance.[6]
Section: Cause and mechanism
The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] Keratin 1 is associated with the variants affecting the palms and soles.[6] Keratin 10 is associated with the variants in which these are unaffected.[6]
Section: History
EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]
Section: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is by its appearance, skin biopsy, and genetic testing.[6] The condition can be diagnosed via exam that reveals; generalized redness; thick, generally dark, scales that tend to form parallel rows of spines or ridges, especially near large joints; the skin is fragile and blisters easily following trauma; extent of blistering and amount of scale is variable.[citation needed]
Section: Epidemiology
The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Treatment
Treatment includes applying thick moisturisers.[5] Other therapies include topical and oral retinoids.[5] These include topical N-acetylcysteine, liarozole, and calcipotriol.[6] Bacterial colonisation of skin may be reduced by use of antibacterial soaps, chlorhexidine, and dilute sodium hypochlorite baths.[6]

Section: Introduction
Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI),[a] is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures, strong body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] The two main types are divided into one involving palms and soles and the other without.[6] EI is caused by a genetic mutation.[6] The condition involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[5][6] The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
EI is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures,  body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] Complications include infection and joint problems.[6] Affected newborns are particularly at risk of dehydration, sepsis, and electrolyte imbalance.[6]
Section: Cause and mechanism
The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] Keratin 1 is associated with the variants affecting the palms and soles.[6] Keratin 10 is associated with the variants in which these are unaffected.[6]
Section: History
EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]
Section: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is by its appearance, skin biopsy, and genetic testing.[6] The condition can be diagnosed via exam that reveals; generalized redness; thick, generally dark, scales that tend to form parallel rows of spines or ridges, especially near large joints; the skin is fragile and blisters easily following trauma; extent of blistering and amount of scale is variable.[citation needed]
Section: Epidemiology
The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Treatment
Treatment includes applying thick moisturisers.[5] Other therapies include topical and oral retinoids.[5] These include topical N-acetylcysteine, liarozole, and calcipotriol.[6] Bacterial colonisation of skin may be reduced by use of antibacterial soaps, chlorhexidine, and dilute sodium hypochlorite baths.[6]

Section: Introduction
Hyperkeratosis is thickening of the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis, or skin), often associated with the presence of an abnormal quantity of keratin,[1] and is usually accompanied by an increase in the granular layer. As the corneum layer normally varies greatly in thickness in different sites, some experience is needed to assess minor degrees of hyperkeratosis. It can be caused by vitamin A deficiency or chronic exposure to arsenic. Hyperkeratosis can also be caused by B-Raf inhibitor drugs such as vemurafenib and dabrafenib.[2] It can be treated with urea-containing creams, which dissolve the intercellular matrix of the cells of the stratum corneum, promoting desquamation of scaly skin, eventually resulting in softening of hyperkeratotic areas.[3]
Section: Types
This condition has been shown in several small-scale studies to respond well to supplementation with vitamins and fats rich in essential fatty acids. Deficiencies of vitamin E,[4] vitamin A, and B-complex vitamins have been implicated in causing the condition.[5] Follicular hyperkeratosis is also a symptom in inherited collagen-related diseases of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and Bethlem myopathy. Plantar hyperkeratosis is hyperkeratosis of the sole of the foot. It is recommended to surgically remove the dead skin, to provide symptomatic relief. Hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola is an uncommon benign, asymptomatic, acquired condition of unknown pathogenesis.[6]: 636 Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (also known as "Bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma,"[7] "Bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma,"[8]: 482  or "bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma of Brocq"[9]) is a rare skin disease in the ichthyosis family, affecting around 1 in 250,000 people. It involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[6]: 562 [10] Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis, a rare cutaneous condition, with about half of cases being familial Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis, a rare cutaneous condition, with about half of cases being familial Focal acral hyperkeratosis (also known as "Acrokeratoelastoidosis lichenoides,") is a late-onset keratoderma, inherited as an autosomal dominant condition, characterized by oval or polygonal crateriform papules developing along the border of the hands, feet, and wrists.[8]: 509 Keratosis pilaris appears similar to gooseflesh, is usually asymptomatic and may be treated by moisturizing the skin.[11] Hyperkeratosis lenticularis perstans (also known as "Flegel's disease"[7]) is a cutaneous condition characterized by rough, yellow-brown keratotic, flat-topped papules.[6]: 639 [7]

Section: Types
Hereditary benign intraepithelial dyskeratosis is a rare type of genodermatosis that may occur in infancy and early childhood, its symptoms often appear in the patients' eyes and mouths.[17] The patients' eyes appear red due to the dilatation of superficial vessels and appearance of conjunctival plaques in their eyes, patients may have variable-size, thick, soft and white plaques in their mouth.[17] Spring is an acute episode of symptoms, such as itching, erythema, photophobia and so on.[17] Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is a rare genodermatosis which is also referred to as disorder of cornification type 3 and bullous congenital ichthyosiform erthroderma, affecting almost 1 per 200,000 - 300,000 people.[18] They also stated that its clinical manifestations often begin at birth with large rashes all over the body, and the patients' skin will be so sensitive that even mild wounds can cause blisters and peeling. Potential complications of this disease include electrolyte disturbances, sepsis and so on.[18] Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is a rare genodermatosis which is also known as Clouston syndrome. The patients' nails may be too thick, too brittle, too bent or have different colors, their hair also appear mottled, sparse and other abnormalities.[19] These symptoms often begin when the patient is an infant.[19]
Section: Therapy
For epidermolysis bullosa, daily care is important. When treating a wound, keep it clean and reduce friction, the bandages and dressing used must be non-sticky and gentle, and the patient should wear loose clothing to avoid damaging the wound.[13][14] The treatment of Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is mainly control and alleviate symptoms, and good nursing can reduce the incidence of complications like electrolyte disturbances and sepsis.[18] To improve the look and feeling of the skin, patients can apply a cream containing alpha hydroxy acids, glycerol and urea, and if necessary, patients can use antibiotics to control secondary infections.[18] There is no radical therapeutic method for pachyonychia congenita, but some care can ease the symptoms.[16] Patients can polish and trim thickened nails, some of them can use retinoids to relieve symptoms but it may increase pain.[16]
Section: Introduction
Genodermatosis is a hereditary skin disease with three inherited modes including single gene inheritance, multiple gene inheritance and chromosome inheritance.[1] There are many different types of genodermatosis; the prevalence of genodermatosis ranges from 1 per 6000 people to 1 per 500,000 people.[2] Genodermatosis has influence on the texture, color and structure of skin cuticle and connective tissue. Specific lesion site and clinical manifestations on the body vary depending on the type.[3] In spite of the variety and complexity of genodermatosis, there are still some common methods that can help people diagnose.[4] After diagnosis, different types of genodermatosis require different levels of therapy including interventions, nursing interventions and treatments.[5] Among that, research of therapy for some new, complex and rare types are still in the developing stage.[6] The impact of genodermatosis not only can be seen in the body but also can be seen in all aspects of patients' life, including but not limited to psychological, family life, economic conditions and social activities.[5][7] Accordingly, the patients need treatment, support and help in these areas.[5]

llm.short_answer: A rare genetic skin disorder causing thickened, scaly skin on the palms and soles
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_5], [GG_9]. Detailed explanation: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is a rare skin disorder characterized by the clumping of keratin filaments that leads to abnormal skin structure and scaling. In some cases, particularly those associated with keratin 1 mutations, this condition manifests as palmoplantar keratoderma, where the hyperkeratosis (thickening of the skin) is predominantly confined to the palms and soles.

llm.long_answer: Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1], [GG_13]. Detailed explanation: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is a rare genetic skin disorder, also known as epidermolytic ichthyosis or bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, that typically presents in newborns with skin redness, blistering, erosions, and later the development of thick scales (hyperkeratosis). The condition has two main types: one in which mutations (particularly in keratin 1) lead to hyperkeratosis affecting the palms and soles (palmoplantar hyperkeratosis), and another variant, associated with keratin 10 mutations, where the palms and soles are unaffected.

Hereditary benign intraepithelial dyskeratosis is a rare type of genodermatosis that may occur in infancy and early childhood, its symptoms often appear in the patients' eyes and mouths.[17] The patients' eyes appear red due to the dilatation of superficial vessels and appearance of conjunctival plaques in their eyes, patients may have variable-size, thick, soft and white plaques in their mouth.[17] Spring is an acute episode of symptoms, such as itching, erythema, photophobia and so on.[17] Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is a rare genodermatosis which is also referred to as disorder of cornification type 3 and bullous congenital ichthyosiform erthroderma, affecting almost 1 per 200,000 - 300,000 people.[18] They also stated that its clinical manifestations often begin at birth with large rashes all over the body, and the patients' skin will be so sensitive that even mild wounds can cause blisters and peeling. Potential complications of this disease include electrolyte disturbances, sepsis and so on.[18] Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is a rare genodermatosis which is also known as Clouston syndrome. The patients' nails may be too thick, too brittle, too bent or have different colors, their hair also appear mottled, sparse and other abnormalities.[19] These symptoms often begin when the patient is an infant.[19]
Section: Therapy
For epidermolysis bullosa, daily care is important. When treating a wound, keep it clean and reduce friction, the bandages and dressing used must be non-sticky and gentle, and the patient should wear loose clothing to avoid damaging the wound.[13][14] The treatment of Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is mainly control and alleviate symptoms, and good nursing can reduce the incidence of complications like electrolyte disturbances and sepsis.[18] To improve the look and feeling of the skin, patients can apply a cream containing alpha hydroxy acids, glycerol and urea, and if necessary, patients can use antibiotics to control secondary infections.[18] There is no radical therapeutic method for pachyonychia congenita, but some care can ease the symptoms.[16] Patients can polish and trim thickened nails, some of them can use retinoids to relieve symptoms but it may increase pain.[16]
Section: Introduction
Genodermatosis is a hereditary skin disease with three inherited modes including single gene inheritance, multiple gene inheritance and chromosome inheritance.[1] There are many different types of genodermatosis; the prevalence of genodermatosis ranges from 1 per 6000 people to 1 per 500,000 people.[2] Genodermatosis has influence on the texture, color and structure of skin cuticle and connective tissue. Specific lesion site and clinical manifestations on the body vary depending on the type.[3] In spite of the variety and complexity of genodermatosis, there are still some common methods that can help people diagnose.[4] After diagnosis, different types of genodermatosis require different levels of therapy including interventions, nursing interventions and treatments.[5] Among that, research of therapy for some new, complex and rare types are still in the developing stage.[6] The impact of genodermatosis not only can be seen in the body but also can be seen in all aspects of patients' life, including but not limited to psychological, family life, economic conditions and social activities.[5][7] Accordingly, the patients need treatment, support and help in these areas.[5]


- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_2] - Information about: Hyperkeratosis - epidermolytic hyperkeratosis
Section: Introduction
Hyperkeratosis is thickening of the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis, or skin), often associated with the presence of an abnormal quantity of keratin,[1] and is usually accompanied by an increase in the granular layer. As the corneum layer normally varies greatly in thickness in different sites, some experience is needed to assess minor degrees of hyperkeratosis. It can be caused by vitamin A deficiency or chronic exposure to arsenic. Hyperkeratosis can also be caused by B-Raf inhibitor drugs such as vemurafenib and dabrafenib.[2] It can be treated with urea-containing creams, which dissolve the intercellular matrix of the cells of the stratum corneum, promoting desquamation of scaly skin, eventually resulting in softening of hyperkeratotic areas.[3]
Section: Types
This condition has been shown in several small-scale studies to respond well to supplementation with vitamins and fats rich in essential fatty acids. Deficiencies of vitamin E,[4] vitamin A, and B-complex vitamins have been implicated in causing the condition.[5] Follicular hyperkeratosis is also a symptom in inherited collagen-related diseases of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and Bethlem myopathy. Plantar hyperkeratosis is hyperkeratosis of the sole of the foot. It is recommended to surgically remove the dead skin, to provide symptomatic relief. Hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola is an uncommon benign, asymptomatic, acquired condition of unknown pathogenesis.[6]: 636 Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (also known as "Bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma,"[7] "Bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma,"[8]: 482  or "bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma of Brocq"[9]) is a rare skin disease in the ichthyosis family, affecting around 1 in 250,000 people. It involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[6]: 562 [10] Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis, a rare cutaneous condition, with about half of cases being familial Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis, a rare cutaneous condition, with about half of cases being familial Focal acral hyperkeratosis (also known as "Acrokeratoelastoidosis lichenoides,") is a late-onset keratoderma, inherited as an autosomal dominant condition, characterized by oval or polygonal crateriform papules developing along the border of the hands, feet, and wrists.[8]: 509 Keratosis pilaris appears similar to gooseflesh, is usually asymptomatic and may be treated by moisturizing the skin.[11] Hyperkeratosis lenticularis perstans (also known as "Flegel's disease"[7]) is a cutaneous condition characterized by rough, yellow-brown keratotic, flat-topped papules.[6]: 639 [7]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis - epidermolytic hyperkeratosis
Section: Introduction
Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI),[a] is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures, strong body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] The two main types are divided into one involving palms and soles and the other without.[6] EI is caused by a genetic mutation.[6] The condition involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[5][6] The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
EI is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures,  body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] Complications include infection and joint problems.[6] Affected newborns are particularly at risk of dehydration, sepsis, and electrolyte imbalance.[6]
Section: Cause and mechanism
The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] Keratin 1 is associated with the variants affecting the palms and soles.[6] Keratin 10 is associated with the variants in which these are unaffected.[6]
Section: History
EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]
Section: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is by its appearance, skin biopsy, and genetic testing.[6] The condition can be diagnosed via exam that reveals; generalized redness; thick, generally dark, scales that tend to form parallel rows of spines or ridges, especially near large joints; the skin is fragile and blisters easily following trauma; extent of blistering and amount of scale is variable.[citation needed]
Section: Epidemiology
The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Treatment
Treatment includes applying thick moisturisers.[5] Other therapies include topical and oral retinoids.[5] These include topical N-acetylcysteine, liarozole, and calcipotriol.[6] Bacterial colonisation of skin may be reduced by use of antibacterial soaps, chlorhexidine, and dilute sodium hypochlorite baths.[6]

Hereditary benign intraepithelial dyskeratosis is a rare type of genodermatosis that may occur in infancy and early childhood, its symptoms often appear in the patients' eyes and mouths.[17] The patients' eyes appear red due to the dilatation of superficial vessels and appearance of conjunctival plaques in their eyes, patients may have variable-size, thick, soft and white plaques in their mouth.[17] Spring is an acute episode of symptoms, such as itching, erythema, photophobia and so on.[17] Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is a rare genodermatosis which is also referred to as disorder of cornification type 3 and bullous congenital ichthyosiform erthroderma, affecting almost 1 per 200,000 - 300,000 people.[18] They also stated that its clinical manifestations often begin at birth with large rashes all over the body, and the patients' skin will be so sensitive that even mild wounds can cause blisters and peeling. Potential complications of this disease include electrolyte disturbances, sepsis and so on.[18] Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is a rare genodermatosis which is also known as Clouston syndrome. The patients' nails may be too thick, too brittle, too bent or have different colors, their hair also appear mottled, sparse and other abnormalities.[19] These symptoms often begin when the patient is an infant.[19]
Section: Therapy
For epidermolysis bullosa, daily care is important. When treating a wound, keep it clean and reduce friction, the bandages and dressing used must be non-sticky and gentle, and the patient should wear loose clothing to avoid damaging the wound.[13][14] The treatment of Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is mainly control and alleviate symptoms, and good nursing can reduce the incidence of complications like electrolyte disturbances and sepsis.[18] To improve the look and feeling of the skin, patients can apply a cream containing alpha hydroxy acids, glycerol and urea, and if necessary, patients can use antibiotics to control secondary infections.[18] There is no radical therapeutic method for pachyonychia congenita, but some care can ease the symptoms.[16] Patients can polish and trim thickened nails, some of them can use retinoids to relieve symptoms but it may increase pain.[16]
Section: Introduction
Genodermatosis is a hereditary skin disease with three inherited modes including single gene inheritance, multiple gene inheritance and chromosome inheritance.[1] There are many different types of genodermatosis; the prevalence of genodermatosis ranges from 1 per 6000 people to 1 per 500,000 people.[2] Genodermatosis has influence on the texture, color and structure of skin cuticle and connective tissue. Section: Introduction
Hyperkeratosis is thickening of the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis, or skin), often associated with the presence of an abnormal quantity of keratin,[1] and is usually accompanied by an increase in the granular layer. As the corneum layer normally varies greatly in thickness in different sites, some experience is needed to assess minor degrees of hyperkeratosis. Section: Introduction
Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI),[a] is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures, strong body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] The two main types are divided into one involving palms and soles and the other without.[6] EI is caused by a genetic mutation.[6] The condition involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[5][6] The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
EI is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures,  body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] Complications include infection and joint problems.[6] Affected newborns are particularly at risk of dehydration, sepsis, and electrolyte imbalance.[6]
Section: Cause and mechanism
The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] Keratin 1 is associated with the variants affecting the palms and soles.[6] Keratin 10 is associated with the variants in which these are unaffected.[6]
Section: History
EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]
Section: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is by its appearance, skin biopsy, and genetic testing.[6] The condition can be diagnosed via exam that reveals; generalized redness; thick, generally dark, scales that tend to form parallel rows of spines or ridges, especially near large joints; the skin is fragile and blisters easily following trauma; extent of blistering and amount of scale is variable.[citation needed]
Section: Epidemiology
The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Treatment
Treatment includes applying thick moisturisers.[5] Other therapies include topical and oral retinoids.[5] These include topical N-acetylcysteine, liarozole, and calcipotriol.[6] Bacterial colonisation of skin may be reduced by use of antibacterial soaps, chlorhexidine, and dilute sodium hypochlorite baths.[6]

Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI),[a] is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures, strong body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] The two main types are divided into one involving palms and soles and the other without.[6] EI is caused by a genetic mutation.[6] The condition involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[5][6] The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
EI is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures,  body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] Complications include infection and joint problems.[6] Affected newborns are particularly at risk of dehydration, sepsis, and electrolyte imbalance.[6]
Section: Cause and mechanism

EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]

The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]

Treatment includes applying thick moisturisers.[5] Other therapies include topical and oral retinoids.[5] These include topical N-acetylcysteine, liarozole, and calcipotriol.[6] Bacterial colonisation of skin may be reduced by use of antibacterial soaps, chlorhexidine, and dilute sodium hypochlorite baths.[6]

The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]

Section: Cause and mechanism
The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] Keratin 1 is associated with the variants affecting the palms and soles.[6] Keratin 10 is associated with the variants in which these are unaffected.[6]
Section: History
EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]
Section: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is by its appearance, skin biopsy, and genetic testing.[6] The condition can be diagnosed via exam that reveals; generalized redness; thick, generally dark, scales that tend to form parallel rows of spines or ridges, especially near large joints; the skin is fragile and blisters easily following trauma; extent of blistering and amount of scale is variable.[citation needed]
Section: Epidemiology
The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Treatment
Treatment includes applying thick moisturisers.[5] Other therapies include topical and oral retinoids.[5] These include topical N-acetylcysteine, liarozole, and calcipotriol.[6] Bacterial colonisation of skin may be reduced by use of antibacterial soaps, chlorhexidine, and dilute sodium hypochlorite baths.[6]

Section: Types

Section: Introduction
Hyperkeratosis is thickening of the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis, or skin), often associated with the presence of an abnormal quantity of keratin,[1] and is usually accompanied by an increase in the granular layer. As the corneum layer normally varies greatly in thickness in different sites, some experience is needed to assess minor degrees of hyperkeratosis. It can be caused by vitamin A deficiency or chronic exposure to arsenic. Hyperkeratosis can also be caused by B-Raf inhibitor drugs such as vemurafenib and dabrafenib.[2] It can be treated with urea-containing creams, which dissolve the intercellular matrix of the cells of the stratum corneum, promoting desquamation of scaly skin, eventually resulting in softening of hyperkeratotic areas.[3]
Section: Types
This condition has been shown in several small-scale studies to respond well to supplementation with vitamins and fats rich in essential fatty acids. Deficiencies of vitamin E,[4] vitamin A, and B-complex vitamins have been implicated in causing the condition.[5] Follicular hyperkeratosis is also a symptom in inherited collagen-related diseases of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and Bethlem myopathy. Plantar hyperkeratosis is hyperkeratosis of the sole of the foot. It is recommended to surgically remove the dead skin, to provide symptomatic relief. The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] Keratin 1 is associated with the variants affecting the palms and soles.[6] Keratin 10 is associated with the variants in which these are unaffected.[6]

EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]

The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]

Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI),[a] is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures, strong body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] The two main types are divided into one involving palms and soles and the other without.[6] EI is caused by a genetic mutation.[6] The condition involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[5][6] The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Signs and symptoms
EI is a severe form of dry scaly skin, that initially presents with redness, blisters, erosions, and peeling in a newborn baby.[5][6] Hyperkeratosis typically develops several months later.[6] Other symptoms include itch, painful fissures,  body odor, and absence of sweat.[6] Symptoms vary in severity and extent of skin involvement.[5] Complications include infection and joint problems.[6] Affected newborns are particularly at risk of dehydration, sepsis, and electrolyte imbalance.[6]
Section: Cause and mechanism
The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] The condition is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.[6] To a lesser extent, a recessive form exists.[5] It is caused by genetic mutations in the genes encoding the proteins keratin 1 or keratin 10, resulting in disruption of the structure of the epidermis.[6] Keratin 1 is associated with the variants affecting the palms and soles.[6] Keratin 10 is associated with the variants in which these are unaffected.[6]
Section: History
EI was first classified by its presence or absence in the palms and soles by DiGiovanna and Bale in 1994.[6][8]
Section: Diagnosis
Diagnosis is by its appearance, skin biopsy, and genetic testing.[6] The condition can be diagnosed via exam that reveals; generalized redness; thick, generally dark, scales that tend to form parallel rows of spines or ridges, especially near large joints; the skin is fragile and blisters easily following trauma; extent of blistering and amount of scale is variable.[citation needed]
Section: Epidemiology
The condition is rare, affecting around 1 in 200,000 to 300,000 babies.[6]
Section: Treatment
Treatment includes applying thick moisturisers.[5] Other therapies include topical and oral retinoids.[5] These include topical N-acetylcysteine, liarozole, and calcipotriol.[6] Bacterial colonisation of skin may be reduced by use of antibacterial soaps, chlorhexidine, and dilute sodium hypochlorite baths.[6]

Section: Introduction
Hyperkeratosis is thickening of the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis, or skin), often associated with the presence of an abnormal quantity of keratin,[1] and is usually accompanied by an increase in the granular layer. As the corneum layer normally varies greatly in thickness in different sites, some experience is needed to assess minor degrees of hyperkeratosis. It can be caused by vitamin A deficiency or chronic exposure to arsenic. Hyperkeratosis can also be caused by B-Raf inhibitor drugs such as vemurafenib and dabrafenib.[2] It can be treated with urea-containing creams, which dissolve the intercellular matrix of the cells of the stratum corneum, promoting desquamation of scaly skin, eventually resulting in softening of hyperkeratotic areas.[3]
Section: Types
This condition has been shown in several small-scale studies to respond well to supplementation with vitamins and fats rich in essential fatty acids. Deficiencies of vitamin E,[4] vitamin A, and B-complex vitamins have been implicated in causing the condition.[5] Follicular hyperkeratosis is also a symptom in inherited collagen-related diseases of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and Bethlem myopathy. Plantar hyperkeratosis is hyperkeratosis of the sole of the foot. It is recommended to surgically remove the dead skin, to provide symptomatic relief. Hyperkeratosis of the nipple and areola is an uncommon benign, asymptomatic, acquired condition of unknown pathogenesis.[6]: 636 Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (also known as "Bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma,"[7] "Bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma,"[8]: 482  or "bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma of Brocq"[9]) is a rare skin disease in the ichthyosis family, affecting around 1 in 250,000 people. It involves the clumping of keratin filaments.[6]: 562 [10] Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis, a rare cutaneous condition, with about half of cases being familial Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis, a rare cutaneous condition, with about half of cases being familial Focal acral hyperkeratosis (also known as "Acrokeratoelastoidosis lichenoides,") is a late-onset keratoderma, inherited as an autosomal dominant condition, characterized by oval or polygonal crateriform papules developing along the border of the hands, feet, and wrists.[8]: 509 Keratosis pilaris appears similar to gooseflesh, is usually asymptomatic and may be treated by moisturizing the skin.[11] Hyperkeratosis lenticularis perstans (also known as "Flegel's disease"[7]) is a cutaneous condition characterized by rough, yellow-brown keratotic, flat-topped papules.[6]: 639 [7]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_3] - Information about: Genodermatosis - epidermolytic hyperkeratosis
Section: Types
Hereditary benign intraepithelial dyskeratosis is a rare type of genodermatosis that may occur in infancy and early childhood, its symptoms often appear in the patients' eyes and mouths.[17] The patients' eyes appear red due to the dilatation of superficial vessels and appearance of conjunctival plaques in their eyes, patients may have variable-size, thick, soft and white plaques in their mouth.[17] Spring is an acute episode of symptoms, such as itching, erythema, photophobia and so on.[17] Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is a rare genodermatosis which is also referred to as disorder of cornification type 3 and bullous congenital ichthyosiform erthroderma, affecting almost 1 per 200,000 - 300,000 people.[18] They also stated that its clinical manifestations often begin at birth with large rashes all over the body, and the patients' skin will be so sensitive that even mild wounds can cause blisters and peeling. Potential complications of this disease include electrolyte disturbances, sepsis and so on.[18] Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is a rare genodermatosis which is also known as Clouston syndrome. The patients' nails may be too thick, too brittle, too bent or have different colors, their hair also appear mottled, sparse and other abnormalities.[19] These symptoms often begin when the patient is an infant.[19]
Section: Therapy
For epidermolysis bullosa, daily care is important. When treating a wound, keep it clean and reduce friction, the bandages and dressing used must be non-sticky and gentle, and the patient should wear loose clothing to avoid damaging the wound.[13][14] The treatment of Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is mainly control and alleviate symptoms, and good nursing can reduce the incidence of complications like electrolyte disturbances and sepsis.[18] To improve the look and feeling of the skin, patients can apply a cream containing alpha hydroxy acids, glycerol and urea, and if necessary, patients can use antibiotics to control secondary infections.[18] There is no radical therapeutic method for pachyonychia congenita, but some care can ease the symptoms.[16] Patients can polish and trim thickened nails, some of them can use retinoids to relieve symptoms but it may increase pain.[16]
Section: Introduction
Genodermatosis is a hereditary skin disease with three inherited modes including single gene inheritance, multiple gene inheritance and chromosome inheritance.[1] There are many different types of genodermatosis; the prevalence of genodermatosis ranges from 1 per 6000 people to 1 per 500,000 people.[2] Genodermatosis has influence on the texture, color and structure of skin cuticle and connective tissue. Specific lesion site and clinical manifestations on the body vary depending on the type.[3] In spite of the variety and complexity of genodermatosis, there are still some common methods that can help people diagnose.[4] After diagnosis, different types of genodermatosis require different levels of therapy including interventions, nursing interventions and treatments.[5] Among that, research of therapy for some new, complex and rare types are still in the developing stage.[6] The impact of genodermatosis not only can be seen in the body but also can be seen in all aspects of patients' life, including but not limited to psychological, family life, economic conditions and social activities.[5][7] Accordingly, the patients need treatment, support and help in these areas.[5]

Section: Introduction
Hyperkeratosis is thickening of the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis, or skin), often associated with the presence of an abnormal quantity of keratin,[1] and is usually accompanied by an increase in the granular layer. As the corneum layer normally varies greatly in thickness in different sites, some experience is needed to assess minor degrees of hyperkeratosis. It can be caused by vitamin A deficiency or chronic exposure to arsenic. Hyperkeratosis can also be caused by B-Raf inhibitor drugs such as vemurafenib and dabrafenib.[2] It can be treated with urea-containing creams, which dissolve the intercellular matrix of the cells of the stratum corneum, promoting desquamation of scaly skin, eventually resulting in softening of hyperkeratotic areas.[3]
Section: Types
This condition has been shown in several small-scale studies to respond well to supplementation with vitamins and fats rich in essential fatty acids. Deficiencies of vitamin E,[4] vitamin A, and B-complex vitamins have been implicated in causing the condition.[5] Follicular hyperkeratosis is also a symptom in inherited collagen-related diseases of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and Bethlem myopathy. Plantar hyperkeratosis is hyperkeratosis of the sole of the foot. It is recommended to surgically remove the dead skin, to provide symptomatic relief.
